en: The questions are who the holder is, whether the asset can be inherited, whether the platform can block it after death, whether contractual clauses can bar disposal inter vivos or causa mortis. These are relevant conflicts, and the civil-law framework is well equipped to face them.<1>p. 568</1>
How far does the argument against the license go?
The word buy on the button is not illegal in itself, and you do not need to prove you fully own the item to be protected. What is required is a minimum of stability in what you bought.

Defeating the license argument does not settle everything either. It opens the door, but what happens next still depends on what changed, whether the function was preserved and whether the company kept you properly informed.
Not every digital asset falls into this category. First you need to show that what you use truly depends on an environment governed by the platform, and is not just any digital file.
This does not provide grounds for claiming that the use of the word “buy” is, in itself and in isolation, unlawful.<1>p. 402</1>

Yet even once this trick is barred, the central problem of the IOC remains: how to control, within an enjoyment that continues to exist, the ordinary mutations that erode its functional and symbolic integrity?<1>p. 573</1>

I paid for a draw or a loot box. What do I need to know? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I paid for a draw or a loot box.</1> <2>What do I need to know?</2>

You paid to try your luck, in a loot box or an item draw, and what came out was almost never what you wanted. This is one of the most sensitive issues in game purchases, because the company itself decides the odds, the currency, the rarity and the deadlines.

The institutional discussion thus tends to focus on minimum transparency in the conditions of acquisition, the protection of vulnerable audiences and the control of practices that induce consumption, not out of a wish to moralize the sector, but because the supplier holds the internal criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability, under conditions of low external reconstructibility.<1>p. 494-495</1>
How can you tell whether the draw has become the only path to the item?

A loot box is the purchase of a randomly drawn result, not of a chosen item. The value of what you get comes to depend on internal rules of distribution, availability and rarity that only the company sets, often combined with time windows and signals of scarcity.

One example shows how this works. In a well-known game, the most exclusive skins became available only through draws, with tokens costing 400 units of the game's currency, a very low chance of success, a guarantee only on the eightieth draw and a limited-time sale.

In this setup, most attempts return currency and items you were not looking for, which soften the spending and encourage you to try again. When direct purchase disappears and the draw becomes mandatory, you no longer choose how to reach the item and start paying just to try. This design may come close to tying, which means binding the purchase you want to others you did not want.

The point of greatest sensitivity arises when monetization relies on random mechanisms for obtaining items, often referred to in public debate as loot boxes. In these cases, the utility and value of what was acquired come to depend on internal distribution regimes, availability criteria and limits set by the platform, and are also tied to signals of scarcity, time windows and rarity regimes that make decisions more dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation.<1>p. 494</1>

In this context, Law No. 15,211/2025 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2> provides sufficient normative anchoring to locate the focal point, since it regulates, from the standpoint of protecting children and adolescents, loot boxes as a mechanism of random acquisition upon payment.<3>p. 495</3>

The Sanctum is described as an exclusive shop where the user buys Ancient Sparks for 400 RP and uses them to draw rare content, with a specific “banner” for Exalted skins, as well as time-based rotation and no guaranteed return <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025d)</2>.<3>p. 299</3>

Abusive teleology emerges forcefully once one observes that the system not only bars direct purchase of the main good but turns the acquisition into a functional tying sale with a set of items and internal currencies that, along most consumption trajectories, do not match the player's interest. This economic binding does not occur through any declared obligation of joint purchase, but through the design of the path, in which most results do not deliver the desired good and come back as intermediate rewards, especially currencies and collateral cosmetics, which come to function as symbolic cushions for the spending and as an incentive to keep trying <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024a)</2>.<3>p. 450</3>

It would not be a problem if the option to buy the skin directly at a proportionate and reasonable price were kept. However, by making the path mandatory, the company comes closer to an abusive tying practice than to creating an entertainment experience that genuinely cares about the expectations and wishes of its consumer users.<1>p. 450-451</1>
Which records show how much it cost to try?

Keep the screen that described the draw, with the odds, the guarantee after a set number of attempts, the spending cap and the deadline. The official description itself is important evidence, because it shows that the path to the item was designed as a series of paid attempts, not as a direct purchase.

Because the game's currency sits between your money and the draw, the real cost in reais tends to stay hidden. That is why the statements and emails for each currency purchase help, along with a list of what came out of each attempt.

Proof of the exploitative character does not depend on a subjective reading, because the institutional material itself describes the structure in terms of probability, progression and guarantees per attempt, and even presents an investment cap. The relevant evidence is the admission that access is designed as a trajectory of probabilistic extraction, not as a direct purchase of the good <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024a)</2>.<3>p. 450</3>
What can you demand from the company selling the draw?

The first request is for clear purchase conditions, including the odds, where they exist. That is precisely where the debate on loot boxes usually focuses, along with protecting those who are most vulnerable.

When the draw replaces direct purchase and each attempt turns into serial spending, your complaint can target the whole design, not just one purchase. Depending on the case, this design may be treated as an abusive practice, and the request may include fixing the purchase path, without you having to prove that anyone meant to harm you.
If the draw was presented as a near-certain chance while the result depended on luck, the rules on promises also apply, because the ad is part of the purchase.
Where can you turn when the draw is the same for everyone?

Start with the company itself, asking for the conditions and odds that applied when you bought and for the records of your transactions. The request carries more weight when it is specific rather than a generic demand for all your data.

If the company does not resolve it, the case can go to Procon, the state consumer protection agency, to consumidor.gov.br, the federal government's online complaint platform, or to the Small Claims Court (Juizado Especial Cível), options that the channels page explains. Because the draw is the same for everyone, a flaw in its design tends to affect many people, and a response may come through a collective action or from public consumer protection bodies.
Is every paid draw in a game prohibited?

No. The draw itself is not the problem. The issue arises when it replaces direct purchase at a reasonable price. It also arises when the whole design is geared, above all, to exploiting your dependence rather than to legitimate ends such as security and game balance.

The law prohibits loot boxes in games aimed at children and adolescents or likely to be accessed by them. Within that scope or outside it, consumer law also applies, and the sector's own laws do not replace it.

I work through an app, and the rules changed. Can I ask for anything? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I work through an app, and the rules changed.</1> <2>Can I ask for anything?</2>

You do deliveries or rides through an app and, after a rule change nobody explained, you started getting fewer requests, your earnings fell or a restriction was imposed. What matters is not only whether your account is still active, but whether your place in the app still matches what supported the earnings and the continuity you expected.
How can you tell whether the drop is linked to the app's rules?

The app is what hands out job requests, calculates earnings, assigns ratings, sets priority and imposes restrictions. That is why your income depends on how it organizes this environment, not only on your effort.

Changes to how job requests are distributed, to pricing, to the rules for staying eligible, to incentives or to the weight of ratings may leave your account and the partnership label in place. Even so, they can substantially drain the earnings that made staying worthwhile.

Saying that you are free to switch the app on and off does not settle the question. The freedom to join and leave goes hand in hand with heavy dependence on the rules for access, earnings calculation and reputation that the app controls.
Income does not arise outside the environment and merely pass through it. It depends materially on the environment's architecture.<1>p. 766</1>

Changes to call distribution criteria, pricing parameters, eligibility rules, incentive models or reputational weights may preserve the program's name, the appearance of partnership and even the formal existence of the account, while substantially draining the economic utility that justified joining and sustained the continuity of productive enjoyment.<1>p. 767</1>

Here, the formal freedom to join or leave the environment coexists with intense dependence on the private conditions governing access to demand, earnings calculation, reputation building, performance assessment and continued eligibility in the productive flow.<1>p. 766</1>
Which records of your daily work in the app are worth keeping?

Showing only that your earnings fell or that the account was blocked once is not enough. It helps to keep your request history, changes in pay, messages and performance alerts, the criteria disclosed or withheld, records of restrictions and your ratings.

A drop in earnings is not always a normal risk of the job, because it may stem from an unexplained rule change. And the final penalty usually has a backstory, with alerts, incentives and threats that are worth recording from the start.

It is not enough to show a reduction in earnings or an isolated block. The link between governance mechanism and functional impact has to be reconstructed. This may involve call history, variations in pay, the app's internal communications, performance alerts, criteria disclosed or withheld, records of restrictions, rating patterns and comparative data on how the environment changed.<1>p. 768</1>

There are recurring blind spots here that must be avoided. The first is treating fluctuating earnings as a purely natural risk of the activity, when they may result from an opaque unilateral reconfiguration of the distribution infrastructure. The second is treating the final sanction as an isolated event, without reconstructing the regime of conduct, incentive and threat that preceded it.<1>p. 768</1>
What can you ask for when the app changes the rules?

You may ask the app to preserve and disclose the minimum records, to explain restrictions in a way that can be checked and to review the criteria it uses to restrict. You may also ask for clarity on what determines how job requests are distributed and for the restoration of whatever the change made worse.

Metrics are the numbers the app uses to measure your performance. A significant change to rules, calculations, priority or metrics cannot be justified merely by invoking efficiency, security or optimization. It must be at least minimally verifiable, and that does not require opening up the whole system or putting a judge in charge of running the app.

The most appropriate institutional response will tend to favor the preservation and display of minimum records, duties of verifiable reasoning, review of restriction criteria, intelligibility of the relevant parameters for distributing opportunities and functional restoration of the regime whenever the platform has, by design, degraded the productive utility it offered as infrastructure.<1>p. 768</1>

Significant rule changes, changes in calculation, reconfigurations of priority, redefinitions of metrics or sanctions with material impact cannot be shielded by generic talk of efficiency, security or algorithmic optimization. They must be made minimally verifiable. This does not mean fully opening up the system, nor turning the Judiciary into the platform's technical administrator.<1>p. 767</1>
Where can you take a problem with a work app?

The first step is usually the app's own support channel, in writing, asking for the reason for the change and the criteria behind it. Because the decisive records stay with the company, a lawyer can help you request that they be preserved and disclosed.

If the app says you have no protection because you are a partner who earns money from it, that answer does not settle the matter. In certain cases consumer law may extend to people who use the platform to earn an income. This happens when the platform concentrates control over access, continued participation, visibility and the ability to challenge decisions.

When the same change affects everyone who works through the app, the response may be collective, seeking minimum distribution and priority criteria for all. The Public Prosecutor's Office, the Public Defender's Office and the other options are listed on the channels page.
A partner who uses the infrastructure to generate income does not cease to be vulnerable merely because they earn revenue.<1>p. 778</1>

The CDC may apply not only where there is a classic final acquisition, but also where the platform creates significant functional subjection to a private governance environment that controls, in a concentrated way, access, permanence, visibility, verifiability and challenge.<1>p. 779-780</1>
How far does this protection reach for people who work through apps?

This reading does not decide whether an employment relationship exists, nor does it automatically turn the relationship into an employment contract. It looks at the environment the app provides and at how that environment is governed.

A consumer by equivalence is someone the law treats as a consumer because they are exposed to the company's practices, even if they are not the final buyer. Not every partner will be treated this way. The test is demanding, and the Superior Court of Justice (STJ), the court with the final word on consumer law, treats this extension as an exception.

The central point is not merely to assert algorithmic subordination in the abstract, nor to automatically reclassify the whole relationship under the traditional categories of the employment contract. For the purposes of this typology, the focus is on the supply regime.<1>p. 766</1>
The criterion remains demanding. Not every participant in a platform ecosystem will be a consumer by equivalence.<1>p. 780</1>

“Art. 29. For the purposes of this Chapter and the following one, all persons, whether determinable or not, who are exposed to the practices provided for therein are deemed equivalent to consumers” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. In STJ case law, the provision serves as one of the bases of the so-called deepened finalist theory, because it allows, in exceptional cases, the strict reading of final recipient to be relaxed and the CDC to be applied to natural or legal persons who, though not final consumers in the classic sense, are in a situation of vulnerability or exposed to abusive commercial and contractual practices<3>p. 779</3>

I sell on a platform. Does consumer law protect me? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I sell on a platform.</1> <2>Does consumer law protect me?</2>

You sell in an online store or use the platform to make money, and you have heard that consumer law does not apply to you because you run a business. Earning income through the platform does not, by itself, take that protection away. But it reaches you only under certain conditions, which depend on how much control the platform has over your place there.
How can you tell whether your dependence on the platform counts in your favor?

What matters is how far the platform governs your presence on it. The question is whether your continued presence and your ability to understand the environment, reconstruct a dispute and challenge important decisions are in its hands.

There are four strong signs. The platform shapes how the relationship itself is understood, holds the evidence of what it does, allocates opportunities and risks without clarity and decides whether you stay.

Sellers depend on the ranking, the reputation and the prominence that the platform controls. It does not need to expel a seller to take away their real chance to compete, because small advantages in visibility, day after day, can play that role.
Protection is stronger when what the platform sells you, as a product, is a position that is maintained over time within it. One example is your store's place in the shop window.

The peripheral professionalized user does not automatically become the strong party to the relationship just because their activity has an economic purpose. In all these cases, the legally relevant question lies in the density of the platform's governance over their insertion in the ecosystem. If permanence, the intelligibility of the environment, the reconstruction of the conflict and the challenge of relevant decisions remain concentrated under the platform's private control, the a priori exclusion of the CDC by formal label loses its footing.<1>p. 778</1>

What is asserted is something narrower and more serious. When the platform organizes the very intelligibility of the bond, concentrates the evidence of what it does, opaquely distributes opportunities and risks and conditions the continuity of the subject's insertion in the environment, the automatic exclusion of consumer protection by reference to nominal appearances of professionalism or partnership becomes methodologically poor and normatively dangerous.<1>p. 780</1>

In markets of this nature, internal preferencing, self-preferencing, informational barriers, capture of competitive intelligence and opaque discrimination do not necessarily depend on overt acts of exclusion. They may operate through structural micro-advantages, produced by the continuous administration of the visibility, comparability and intelligibility of the ecosystem.<1>p. 770</1>

Once the applicability of art. 29 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> is admitted to qualify legal persons in a factual position of vulnerability, the regime proves fully pertinent when the immaterial object in question is the enjoyment bundle in a sustained position exploited as a product in the B2B market by the holder and offered, through the marketplace platform, to the seller (vendedor).<3>p. 434</3>
Which records of your store are worth keeping?

The platform can adjust visibility, reputation scores, recommendations and return rules. It can also adjust anti-fraud rules and the way disputes are resolved, and all of this changes your risk and your costs without any explicit cutoff. That is why it is worth keeping a dated record of your reputation, the position of your listings in search and every notice of a rule change.

Sales records, ratings and decisions are held by the platform. It is also worth keeping the penalties you receive, the reason given, the appeal route offered and the replies from customer service, because this is the evidence you can actually get.

Modulations in visibility algorithms, reputational metrics, recommendation patterns, return policies, anti-fraud rules and dispute parameters can reconfigure risks, transaction costs and the practical viability of choices without taking the form of an explicit interruption.<1>p. 487</1>

Structural dependence manifests itself through the concentration, within the platform, of transaction records, reputational credentials and decision-making instances, intensifying asymmetries of intelligibility and agency.<1>p. 487</1>
What can a seller ask of the platform?

The request may include minimum clarity about the criteria that decide the order of offers and about the preference the platform gives to some of them. It may also include oversight of changes that push your position down without excluding you, and a careful look at how it uses the data it collects while intermediating sales.

When consumer law reaches sellers, it applies above all to the platform's commercial practices and to the contract clauses. When you are penalized, it also matters that there is a reason you can check and a real way to challenge it.

Whenever the platform, in organizing enjoyment, also comes to organize in an opaque and asymmetric manner the perceptible conditions of competition within the ecosystem, there should be a requirement of controllability compatible with the dual dimension of the problem. This means, at the least, minimum auditability over relevant ranking criteria, intelligibility about prominence and preferencing practices, control of changes that deform the functional equivalence of competitive permanence and a non-naive reading of the use of data obtained through the very position of intermediation.<1>p. 773</1>
[...] the Court describes art. 29 as bearing its own very broad concept of consumer by equivalence, especially aimed at the chapters on commercial practices and contractual protection<1>p. 779</1>
Where can a seller take the complaint?

The first step is usually the platform's channel for sellers, in writing and with screenshots saved. Since a seller's protection depends on showing the dependence and the test is demanding, a lawyer can help you see whether your case qualifies.

When the rule change affects all sellers at the same time, because it comes from the platform's design, the response may be collective. The matter may also concern competition law, which looks after fair competition among sellers.
The platform that governs the user's experience governs, at the same time, the perceptible field in which competition becomes possible, legible and economically effective.<1>p. 769</1>
When does a seller fall outside consumer law?

Not every seller or partner will be treated as a consumer by equivalence, who is the person the law protects as a consumer for being exposed to the company's practices. And not every relationship carried out through technology attracts consumer law.

Protection also does not erase the difference between consumer and company. The Superior Court of Justice (STJ), the court that has the final word on consumer law, treats this extension as an exception. It applies above all to a company that contracts something outside its own area of activity.
And when the platform only sells advertising space and help finding customers, without controlling the sales that follow, this reading does not apply, in principle.

“Art. 29. For the purposes of this Chapter and the following one, all persons, determinable or not, exposed to the practices provided for therein are equated to consumers” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 779</3>

The criterion remains demanding. Not every participant in a platform ecosystem will be a consumer by equivalence. Not every relationship economically mediated by technology will justify application of the CDC.<1>p. 780</1>
The point is not to dissolve every distinction between consumer and economic agent.<1>p. 779</1>

[...] and from it derives the possibility of equating the vulnerable legal person, especially when it acts outside its core specialty, as a way of preventing formal parity from neutralizing the material protection of the CDC.<1>p. 779</1>

<1>Rights</1>
Your rights

When what you buy only exists inside a platform, the sale does not end at the click. The company keeps maintaining, changing and controlling what you use, and that is why it carries duties that stay with the purchase for as long as it lasts. The relationship stops centering on the contract you accepted one day and comes to center on the use you make, every day, of what you bought.
Below are the main duties, one for each situation. For each one you will find when it arises, what the platform owes, what helps show the problem, what you can ask for and how far that goes.

One word of caution. None of this is a ready-made formula or a guarantee of results, because each case depends on what happened, on what can be shown and on how the person deciding reads the facts. What changes is how the conflict is told, which stops being an isolated episode and becomes a matter of how the platform supplies what it sold.
Enjoyment, here, does not appear as an accidental effect of a formally concluded contract, but as the material core of the consumer relationship.<1>p. 717-718</1>
In continuous consumption, the acquisition opens a position in the ecosystem rather than a delivery exhausted in an instant.<1>p. 428</1>
The way the conflict is narrated changes, because attention shifts from the isolated event to the supply program.<1>p. 788</1>

Whenever the utility consumed depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and changeable by private governance, with an impact on access, permanence, intelligibility or updating of the experience, the IOC's field of application will be established.<1>p. 743</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to ensure enjoyment that is functionally accessible, intelligible and preserved within the limits of the legitimate mutability of the environment.<1>p. 743</1>

The minimum required evidence concerns demonstrating the structural dependence of the utility on the governed ecosystem, the way the experience is made available and the consumer's concrete position in the bond.<1>p. 743</1>

The resulting legal qualification is that of an immaterial product subject to the regime of art. 3, § 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, without the service dimension of the bond displacing control of enjoyment as the core of supply.<3>p. 743</3>

The possible institutional consequence consists in opening the subsequent filters of the regime, preventing the controversy from being neutralized by the claim of mere provision of a service or of simple formal licensing.<1>p. 743</1>
The service does not disappear, but appears as a way of sustaining, updating and shaping the object of consumption itself.<1>p. 718</1>

The fifth limit is the case in which the core of the conflict lies elsewhere, such as a classic one-off defect, an improper charge, localized misleading advertising or a specific breach of an offer. In these cases, ordinary consumer law dogmatics tends to resolve the dispute with no real gain from invoking the IOC.<1>p. 435</1>
<1>The platform cannot design the experience to keep you from understanding</1><2>The platform cannot design the experience to keep you from understanding</2>

Whenever expectation, perception of value, risk assessment or capacity to challenge depend on signs, interfaces, flows and informational trails controlled by the supplier, there will be legally relevant semiotic vulnerability.<1>p. 744</1>
The term does not designate naivety, credulity or cultural deficiency on the part of the consumer.<1>p. 719</1>
Whoever controls the way in which the object is made intelligible often also controls the records through which that intelligibility can be reconstructed in case of conflict.<1>p. 720</1>
The corresponding duty is not to organize the experience through a structural asymmetry of meaning incompatible with good faith, transparency and legibility of enjoyment.<1>p. 744</1>

The minimum required evidence involves reconstructing the user's journey, the informational architecture of the environment, the communicational saliences, the paths of understanding and the records available to reconstruct how the expectation was formed.<1>p. 744</1>
The first source of support is interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade, confirmation screens<1>p. 607</1>
What is relevant there is not the user's subjective memory<1>p. 607</1>

The possible legal qualification may support abusive practice, informational insufficiency, deceptiveness through ambiguity or relevant omission and, when combined with other elements, grounds for a dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof.<1>p. 744</1>

The institutional consequence consists in bringing the conflict back to the governance of the environment, avoiding moralization of the consumer's conduct and allowing the application of reinforced duties of information, advertising and proof.<1>p. 744</1>
Nor is it a matter of presupposing absolute incapacity in the face of the digital.<1>p. 720</1>
<1>Information has to be of real use</1><2>Information has to be of real use</2>

Whenever the platform replaces legibility with textual excess, strategic dispersion, fragmentation of informational trajectories or merely performative transparency, the duty to inform will have been inadequately met.<1>p. 744</1>

Information, in the CDC, does not fulfill its function just because it exists somewhere, nor because it was deposited in lengthy documents, cross-references, FAQs or update histories that the consumer is unlikely to locate, understand and connect to the impact<1>p. 641</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to provide information that is materially adequate, useful for the decision and verifiable at a later moment of controversy.<1>p. 744</1>

The minimum required evidence requires identifying what was shown, at what moment, with what salience, through which channels and to what extent this organization allowed the consumer to understand what was legally relevant to join, remain or react.<1>p. 744</1>

The legal qualification tends to apply as a defect in the informational quality of the supply, abusive practice through functional obscuring and, depending on the case, support for the invalidity of clauses or limitations incompatible with the legitimately formed expectation.<1>p. 744</1>

The possible institutional consequence includes a duty to correct the communicational arrangement, reinforcement of useful transparency, disclosure orders and restoration of the enjoyment affected by decision-making opacity.<1>p. 744</1>
The point is not to assert that the consumer “did not read” or “did not understand”<1>p. 401</1>
<1>What was promised has to be delivered</1><2>What was promised has to be delivered</2>

Whenever enjoyment is preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences, advertising will materially integrate the offer.<1>p. 744-745</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to ensure correspondence between promise, announced value, concealed costs and the experience actually made available under administered mutability.<1>p. 745</1>

The minimum required evidence involves reconstructing the promotional environment, the communication pieces, the symbolic saliences, the context of presentation of the object and the relation between prior promise and subsequent enjoyment.<1>p. 745</1>
The legal qualification may consist of misleading or abusive advertising, a binding offer, abusive practice through administered ambiguity<1>p. 745</1>

The possible institutional consequence encompasses correction of the offer, functional restoration, injunctive protection over the communication and, depending on the case, invalidation of promotional strategies incompatible with the real experience delivered.<1>p. 745</1>
<1>A relevant change has to leave a trail</1><2>A relevant change has to leave a trail</2>

Whenever relevant changes to access, performance, utility, operating rule or sanction affect enjoyment without preservation of minimum trails of institutional reconstruction, there will be a violation of the parameter of open auditability.<1>p. 745</1>

The corresponding duty of supply is to maintain minimum verifiability over what was changed, when it was changed, on what grounds it was justified and what functionally relevant effects it produced.<1>p. 745</1>
That is why open auditability must be understood as an internal development of the duty to inform and not as an institution foreign to the microsystem.<1>p. 641</1>

A standard of minimum verifiability, compatible with the protection of software and trade secrets, but incompatible with the opaque shielding of execution; a development of the duty to inform, of objective good faith and of facilitating the consumer's defense<1>p. 648</1>
The requirement of open auditability is not to be confused with full disclosure of the source code or with suppression of the technical secrecy of software.<1>p. 643</1>

The minimum required evidence consists of essential logs, history of relevant versions, sanction records, minimum operational justifications, context data and delimited technical elements sufficient to make the controversy cognizable.<1>p. 745</1>

The institutional consequence includes orders to preserve and disclose records, delimited expert examination, presumptions unfavorable to the supplier and control of the lawfulness of the change or sanction based on minimum institutional intelligibility.<1>p. 745</1>
Open auditability is not required for every microscopic adjustment, every cosmetic change or every irrelevant fluctuation of the service.<1>p. 642</1>

It may affect access and permanence, the functional integrity of the object, promised equivalences, the symbolic position of the IOC in the ecosystem, or even the consumer's conditions of proof and challenge.<1>p. 642</1>
<1>If it changes, it must keep the value it had</1><2>If it changes, it must keep the value it had</2>

Whenever the platform changes the experience in a way that degrades, empties or substantially diverts the function that justified the acquisition, there will be a rupture of functional value equivalence.<1>p. 745</1>
The strength of the criterion appears clearly in cases such as removals of relevant features, nerfs that empty out acquired utility<1>p. 637</1>

The consumer remains formally “inside” the ecosystem, still has the account, still sees the object, can still access the platform. Even so, the utility enjoyed may be substantially downgraded<1>p. 635</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to preserve, in substantial terms, the functional, relational and, when legally relevant, symbolic role of the object in the consumer's experience.<1>p. 745</1>

The minimum required evidence requires demonstration of the utility previously incorporated into the bond, of the change that occurred, of the concrete functional impact of the alteration and of the insufficiency of any restoration offered.<1>p. 745-746</1>
The possible legal qualification tends to be a quality defect of the product or service<1>p. 746</1>

The possible institutional consequence prioritizes functional restoration, technical reversal when feasible, equivalent replacement and correction of the form of updating, instead of mere automatic monetization of the loss.<1>p. 746</1>
This does not mean requiring perfect identity between earlier and later versions, nor imposing a freeze on the service.<1>p. 730</1>

What the parameter refuses is not change itself, but its instrumentalization to transfer to the consumer the cost of reconfigurations that destroy or significantly downgrade the acquired utility without compatible restoration.<1>p. 730</1>

Nerfs, removals, reworks, migrations, rule changes, reordering of access, reconfiguration of interfaces and removal of features are usually presented as the natural evolution of the environment. In many cases, in fact, they may be just that.<1>p. 730</1>
<1>A penalty needs a reason and a chance to defend yourself</1><2>A penalty needs a reason and a chance to defend yourself</2>

Whenever access, permanence, visibility or challenge are conditioned by opaque sanctions, selective frictions, excessive costs of reaction or asymmetric reversal mechanisms, there will be an indication of abusive governance of the bond.<1>p. 746</1>

The corresponding duty of supply is to ensure minimally intelligible procedures, verifiable reasoning, a reasonable possibility of challenge and non-arbitrary treatment of the user in the administration of enjoyment.<1>p. 746</1>

The minimum required evidence concerns sanction records, the challenge flow, the criteria mobilized, structural difficulties of reversal and the concrete impacts of the measure on the continuity of the experience.<1>p. 746</1>

The institutional consequence includes reversal or review of sanctions, procedural duties, creation or improvement of challenge mechanisms and, in structurally repetitive cases, correction of the ecosystem's enforcement regime.<1>p. 746</1>

For this reason, they must be controlled by criteria denser than the mere formal existence of sanctioning power. They require verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of challenge.<1>p. 749</1>
Added to this is a reward architecture, with progression and grind systems, and a sanctioning architecture, with bans, restrictions, automated penalties and opaque policies<1>p. 211</1>

[...] including the so-called Virtual Content, takes place under a limited and revocable license, conditioned on compliance with the Terms, and that closing the account entails automatic cancellation of the license and loss of access to the associated content<1>p. 408</1>
<1>When loss is the rule, the problem is the design</1><2>When loss is the rule, the problem is the design</2>

Whenever microfrictions, normalized losses, manufactured urgencies, artificial scarcities, strategic opacity, elastic equivalences and other mechanisms operate in a coordinated way to extract value from vulnerability or to degrade enjoyment as a routine of the environment, there will be a case of abusive teleology.<1>p. 746</1>

It is not a matter of investigating the subjective psychological intention of business agents, nor of moralizing every form of monetization, persuasion or private governance. The focus is on the functional purpose objectively inscribed in the arrangement, as revealed by its replicability, by its internal coherence and by its repeated impact on the consumer's experience.<1>p. 732</1>

The corresponding duty of supply is the duty not to structure the experience around an exploitative purpose incompatible with good faith, transparency, balance and the protection of the enjoyment legitimately incorporated into the relationship.<1>p. 746</1>

The minimum required evidence consists in demonstrating the pattern, its replicability, the coordination among mechanisms of the ecosystem and the relevant impact produced on practical autonomy, intelligibility or utility of the experience.<1>p. 746-747</1>

The institutional consequence goes beyond the redress of isolated episodes and may include reconfiguration of flows, reinforced transparency duties, design correction and structural or collective measures.<1>p. 747</1>
What is controlled is not an inner will, but a recognizable program<1>p. 732</1>
<1>The evidence held by the platform has to come out</1><2>The evidence held by the platform has to come out</2>

Whenever the platform concentrates the essential elements to narrate, demonstrate and reconstruct the conflict, the evidentiary discipline must recognize that verifiability is part of the very legitimate regime of supply.<1>p. 747</1>
The corresponding duty is to preserve and disclose the minimum records necessary to reconstruct the disputed event.<1>p. 747</1>

The minimum required evidence, from the consumer's point of view, consists in a plausible presentation of the harmful experience, of its insertion in the ecosystem and of the accessible context elements<1>p. 747</1>
from the supplier's point of view, it requires the disclosure of trails, logs, histories, versions and technically delimited justifications<1>p. 747</1>

The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to require the consumer to demonstrate in detail facts whose documentary and technical support was never within their reach.<1>p. 736</1>
The possible legal qualification involves dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, presumptions favorable to the consumer and reinforcement of the duty of cooperation<1>p. 747</1>

This does not eliminate the need for plausibility, argumentative linkage or delimitation of the disputed object. What it eliminates is the fiction of symmetry in environments whose very structure operates through asymmetry of meaning and of proof.<1>p. 736</1>
The institutional consequence consists in preventing technical opacity from turning into procedural shielding<1>p. 747</1>
<1>Owning the work is not an excuse for everything</1><2>Owning the work is not an excuse for everything</2>

Whenever the platform invokes exclusive ownership, trade secrets, licensing or the proprietary structure of the ecosystem to resist control of the mode of supply, reconciliation must be made in light of the social function and the constitutional limits on the exercise of private positions.<1>p. 747</1>

On the contrary, it expressly subordinates the legal guarantee of the privilege over industrial inventions and of the protection of industrial creations, trademarks, company names and other distinctive signs to the social interest and to the technological and economic development of the country<1>p. 702</1>

In this scenario, intellectual property appears as an infrastructure of semiotic and technical governance. It not only protects creations, but helps delimit uses, restrict reconfigurations and consolidate the supplier's authority over the conditions of enjoyment<1>p. 130</1>
Licenses and technical restrictions are not treated merely as contractual content<1>p. 54</1>
that delimits what can be used, for how long, under what conditions<1>p. 54</1>
The corresponding duty is to exercise exclusivity without turning it into a shield for absolute opacity, degrading mutability or arbitrary suppression of enjoyment.<1>p. 747</1>

The minimum required evidence concerns the relation between the prerogative invoked and the concrete aspect of the conflict, showing whether the restriction is really necessary to protect the asset or in fact operates as an undue immunization of governance.<1>p. 747</1>
The possible legal qualification preserves the validity of intellectual property on its own plane, but rules out its invocation as a general veto on the application of the CDC.<1>p. 747</1>

institutional consequence consists in reconciling exclusivity and consumer protection through delimited auditability, control of functional equivalence and subjection of the exercise of IP to the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration.<1>p. 748</1>

The right to exploit, close or reorganize an economic activity is not to be confused with a supposed right to annihilate, without duties of transition, preservation or transfer, the functional enjoyment already stabilized in the consumer's sphere.<1>p. 709</1>
<1>The answer should restore what you lost</1><2>The answer should restore what you lost</2>

Whenever the injury affects access, continuity, equivalence, history, relational position or significant density of enjoyment, the legal response must prioritize functional restoration, reserving monetary compensation for cases where restoration is unfeasible or insufficient.<1>p. 748</1>
The corresponding duty is to structure protection in accordance with the nature of the loss, aiming at the affected enjoyment and not only at its residual monetary translation.<1>p. 748</1>

The minimum required evidence involves demonstrating the causal link between the governance mechanism and the functional loss, as well as the technical or institutional possibility of restoration, reversal, equivalent replacement or procedural correction.<1>p. 748</1>

The possible legal qualification varies according to the main incidence of the case, but the institutional consequence should favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history, equivalent functional replacement, governance adjustments, injunctive protection and structural correction when the harm reveals a repeatable pattern<1>p. 748</1>

In these cases, monetary compensation continues to play an important role, whether to reimburse material losses or to recognize non-pecuniary damages when present. What is refused is its transformation into an automatic and preferential response in every case, as if injury to the IOC could always be adequately translated into a figure without regard to the structure of the compromised enjoyment.<1>p. 742</1>

Where can you complain when the platform won't fix the problem?

When talking to the platform gets you nowhere, the law offers other routes, and almost all of them are free. Here are the main ones, with what each one does, what it asks of you and how much time you have.
Information added on November 8, 2026, based on the law and the official channels.<1> It is a later addition to the thesis, which does not deal with complaint channels.</1>
Where do you start?

The first path is usually the company itself, through the customer service channel it offers. It is worth complaining in writing, or in a channel that generates a ticket number, and keeping that number.
This has a legal effect. A complaint made to the company, as long as you can prove you made it, stops the clock on the deadline until the company answers with a clear no.
What Article 26 of the CDC says<1><2>1</2></1>

Art. 26. The right to complain about apparent or easily noticeable defects lapses in: I - thirty days, in the case of supply of services and non-durable products; II - ninety days, in the case of supply of services and durable products. § 1 The lapse period begins to run from the effective delivery of the product or the end of the performance of the services. § 2 The following prevent lapse: I - a complaint demonstrably made by the consumer to the supplier of products and services until the corresponding negative answer, which must be transmitted unequivocally; II - (Vetoed). III - the opening of a civil inquiry, until its closing. § 3 In the case of a hidden defect, the lapse period begins at the moment the defect becomes evident.
Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (Código de Defesa do Consumidor, CDC), Law 8,078/1990, on the <1>Planalto website</1>

§ 2 The following prevent lapse: I - a complaint demonstrably made by the consumer to the supplier of products and services until the corresponding negative answer, which must be transmitted unequivocally;<1>p. 558</1>
How much time do you have to complain?

For a defect that is easy to notice, the Consumer Protection Code gives thirty days when the service or product is not durable, and ninety days when it is durable. The deadline runs from the delivery of the product or the end of the service.

If the problem stays hidden and only shows up later, the deadline starts when it becomes evident. In a service that continues over time, such as a game or an account, the loss may appear little by little, and the count should follow the moment when it can be noticed.
The law does not say in so many words whether a digital item is durable or not. That is why the safest course is to complain within the thirty days and keep proof that you complained.

When the problem causes greater harm, which affects you or your property beyond the item itself, the deadline to claim compensation is five years. It runs from when you learned of the harm and of who caused it.

Art. 27. The claim for redress of damages caused by product-caused or service-caused accidents provided for in Section II of this Chapter is time-barred in five years, the period beginning to run from knowledge of the damage and of its authorship.
I - thirty days, in the case of supply of services and non-durable products; II - ninety days, in the case of supply of services and durable products.<1>p. 558</1>

In continuing relationships, the deadline cannot be used to turn the initial formal delivery into an artificial milestone for the early emptying of consumer protection. The count must be attuned to the real moment of cognizability of the inadequacy, especially when it only emerges in prolonged use or in the supervening deterioration of serviceability<1>p. 558</1>
How does consumidor.gov.br work?
consumidor.gov.br is a free public service of the federal government for resolving consumer disputes over the internet. You register the complaint, and the company answers right there.

To use it, you need a silver or gold level gov.br account. The company also needs to be registered on the site, and its participation is voluntary. If it is not, the site itself lets you suggest that it join.
After registration, the company has up to ten days to answer. Then you have up to twenty days to say whether the problem was solved and to rate the service.
The site does not replace Procon, the Public Defender's Office, the Public Prosecutor's Office or the Small Claims Court, which remain available to you.

A free public service for resolving consumer disputes over the internet, monitored by the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) of the Ministry of Justice.

The company needs to be registered on the site to receive the complaint, and its participation is voluntary. If it is not, the consumer can suggest that it join.
The company has up to 10 days to answer. Afterward, the consumer has up to 20 days to evaluate the answer.

What can Procon do?
Procon is the consumer protection agency of your state or city, and it is part of the national consumer protection system. It serves consumers, processes complaints and oversees consumer relations.
Each Procon has its own channels, which may be in person or online. A complaint at Procon also leaves a record, which helps show later that you tried to solve the problem.
What Article 105 of the CDC says
Art. 105. The National Consumer Protection System (SNDC) comprises the federal, state, Federal District and municipal bodies and the private consumer protection entities.
What Article 4, items II and III, of Decree No. 2,181/1997 says

Art. 4 Within its jurisdiction and competence, the state, Federal District and municipal consumer protection body, created by law specifically for this purpose, shall carry out the activities contained in items II to XII of art. 3 of this Decree and also: [...] II - serve consumers, regularly processing well-founded complaints; III - oversee consumer relations;

When is it worth going to the Small Claims Court?
The Small Claims Court (Juizado Especial Cível) hears less complex cases worth up to forty minimum wages. Filing the claim and getting to the judge's first decision costs nothing.
In cases worth up to twenty minimum wages, you can go without a lawyer. Above that, you need a lawyer, and you also need one if anyone appeals the decision.
What Article 3, item I, of Law No. 9,099/1995 says

Art. 3 The Small Claims Court has competence for conciliation, processing and judgment of civil cases of lesser complexity, considered as such: I - cases whose value does not exceed forty times the minimum wage;
Law No. 9,099/1995, on the <1>Planalto website</1>
What Article 9 of Law No. 9,099/1995 says
Art. 9 In cases worth up to twenty minimum wages, the parties shall appear in person, and may be assisted by a lawyer; in those of higher value, assistance is mandatory.
What Article 54 of Law No. 9,099/1995 says
Art. 54. Access to the Small Claims Court shall not depend, at the first level of jurisdiction, on the payment of court costs, fees or expenses.
What Article 41, paragraph 2, of Law No. 9,099/1995 says
§ 2 On appeal, the parties must be represented by a lawyer.
When is it better to have a lawyer?

A lawyer helps when the amount is high, when the case depends on evidence held by the company or when an appeal is needed. Those who cannot pay are entitled to free legal assistance, which the Public Defender's Office provides.

When the same problem affects many people because it arises from the very design of the service, the answer may be collective. The Public Prosecutor's Office, consumer protection bodies and consumer protection associations can act on behalf of all those affected.
What Article 5, items I, II and IV, of the CDC says

Art. 5 For the execution of the National Consumer Relations Policy, the public authorities shall have the following instruments, among others: I - maintenance of full and free legal assistance for the needy consumer; II - establishment of Consumer Protection Prosecutor's Offices within the Public Prosecutor's Office; [...] IV - creation of Small Claims Courts and Specialized Courts for the resolution of consumer disputes;
What Article 82 of the CDC says

Art. 82. For the purposes of art. 81, sole paragraph, the following have concurrent standing: I - the Public Prosecutor's Office, II - the Union, the States, the Municipalities and the Federal District; III - the entities and bodies of the Public Administration, direct or indirect, even without legal personality, specifically intended to defend the interests and rights protected by this code; IV - associations legally constituted for at least one year and which include among their institutional purposes the defense of the interests and rights protected by this code, with assembly authorization waived.
It is at this point that collective redress ceases to be a mere procedural convenience and imposes itself as a coherent dogmatic consequence of the IOC regime.<1>p. 774</1>

In platform environments, the harmful source may reside in the very design of the supply regime, so that the unity of the problem does not derive primarily from the empirical repetition of episodes, but from the permanence of a single, reiterable and functionally expansive structure producing loss, opacity and asymmetry.<1>p. 774</1>
What should you bring, whichever path you take?
It helps to bring dated screenshots, screen recordings and the purchase, acceptance and confirmation screens. Messages about rarity, time remaining, discount or change also count.

It helps to compare what was promised with what you received and with what changed later. That is why it is worth keeping the ad, the post and the fine print, as well as the ticket number of each contact with the company.

Some of the most important records stay with the company, such as the version history, the transactions and the change notices. In that case, the request may include asking the company to keep and show these records.

The first source of grounding is the interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade, confirmation screens, messages about rarity, equivalence, time remaining, discount, event or change.<1>p. 607</1>

The second source of grounding is the history of offer and mutability. The advertising and institutional promise is compared with the enjoyment actually delivered and with its later changes.<1>p. 607</1>

The third source of grounding concerns advertising and its identifying documents. Promotional pieces, posts, campaigns, influencers, disclaimers, asterisks, cascading cross-references and fine print serve to map how expectation was produced and where the relevant conditions were hidden, diluted or shifted to zones of low visibility.<1>p. 607-608</1>

Whoever controls the service controls, to a large extent, the decisive records of the relationship. Logs, version histories, transactions, interface parameters, change communications and relevant technical documentation tend to remain in the supplier's possession. For this reason, operationalizing the category needs to be accompanied by requests for preservation and disclosure of minimum documentation of the supply.<1>p. 608</1>
Does any of these paths guarantee a result?

None does. Each path gives the company a chance to respond, gives someone outside the case a chance to look at it and gives the law a chance to be applied, but the outcome depends on the evidence and on the particular situation.
This framework is not meant to mechanize the decision or to reduce the complexity of the environment to a rigid formula.<1>p. 748</1>

<1>Why does waiting for the next release also cost you?</1><2>Hypercuratorial anticipation</2>

Before something arrives, the platform is already selling. It announces what is coming, what will disappear, what returns for a limited time and what will become a big event. It releases short trailers, shows the year's roadmap and sets dates.

As a result, expectation comes to count as if it were already here. It becomes a reason to stay, to spend and not to leave, because leaving now would mean missing what is about to arrive. When you buy something under this regime, you are not buying just an item. You are entering a flow, where what matters is also being able to keep counting inside it as the calendar moves on.

Hypercuratorial anticipation designates an economic-semiological technique by which the platform produces a consumable future through continuous curation, defining what will come, what will disappear, what will return and what will be elevated to the status of "event".<1>p. 313</1>
This anticipation is economically relevant for IOCs because it sustains the conversion of expectation into present value, altering the very logic by which the consumer decides and stays.<1>p. 316</1>

When acquiring an immaterial good under this regime, one does not sign on merely to an isolated item, but to a place within a governed flow, in which what “counts” is also the ability to keep counting in the ecosystem as the calendar unfolds.<1>p. 316</1>
<1>Hypercuratorial anticipation</1>

Curation is deciding what will be seen, rewarded and repeated, as a curator does when putting together an exhibition. Here it is so intense, so hyper, that it comes to govern time and to sell the waiting itself. It is not just pretty advertising. It is a way of governing time that turns expectation into a regular way of keeping things valuable. And it makes a promise about the future without giving you, in the same measure, a way to check whether that promise will be kept.

The platform appears as an instance of private administration that organizes enjoyment through architecture, rules and enforcement, defining access, permanence and visibility. This includes both explicit decisions, such as policies and sanctions, and decisions embedded in design, in curation and in the metrics that select what will be seen, rewarded and reproduced<1>p. 262</1>
Hypercuratorial anticipation, in this sense, is not a marketing ornament, but a technique for governing time that monetizes expectation as a regular form of maintaining value.<1>p. 316</1>

This vulnerability is intensified by practices of hypercuratorial anticipation, through which the platform projects images of performance, reward and future experience without offering, in the same measure, real conditions of verification and control by the consumer<1>p. 34</1>
A waiting room with occupied chairs and a clock on the wall. A strong light leaks from under a closed door, and everyone looks at it.
Why does the present become a waiting room?

The present becomes a waiting room. You are always waiting for the next cycle, the next update, the next opportunity. Announcements, previews, roadmaps and seasons deliver the future ahead of time, as if the announcement were already a piece of what was promised.
And the waiting becomes part of what you consume. The platform does not sell only the now. It also sells your staying on while you wait for what is coming.

The present ceases to be the place of a stabilized delivery and becomes a governed antechamber, in which the promise is renewed by announcements, teasers, roadmaps and “seasons” that function as anticipated delivery on the plane of recognition.<1>p. 314</1>
How does the platform decide the pace of the waiting?

There are four moves. Saying what is coming, what will disappear, what returns and what becomes an event. With them the platform decides the pace of things, what is important at each moment and what you should expect.

The effect is to swap the logic of delivery for the logic of the path. The promise becomes a sequence of stages, so that what you have always seems incomplete without the next cycle. The future does not even need to arrive whole. It only needs to remain credible and mobilizing. This way, delivery can be postponed again and again without looking like failure.

Hypercuratorial anticipation designates an economic-semiological technique by which the platform produces a consumable future through continuous curation, defining what will come, what will disappear, what will return and what will be elevated to the status of “event”<1>p. 313</1>
This production governs value itself by deciding rhythms, relevances and expectations within the ecosystem<1>p. 313</1>

The immediate economic effect is the replacement of the “by delivery” logic with a “by directed trajectory” logic. The promise is always reframed as a succession of stages, events and returns, so that enjoyment becomes structurally incomplete without the next cycle.<1>p. 316</1>
The future need not come about in full; it is enough that it remain credible and mobilizing. Thus, delivery can be continually postponed without appearing to be a failure<1>p. 316</1>
What happens when the future becomes the company's calendar?

In announcements about the year's season, a game company presented what it was preparing for the following months as an official sequence of announcements, with a summary, forecasts and links to longer texts. The future stopped being only the players' expectation and became the company's calendar.

The effect is clear. These announcements offer direction and continuity, and this becomes part of the value of keeping an eye on the game. Anyone who stops following feels they will miss out on something.

What is hypercuratorial anticipation?

It is a technique by which the platform produces a consumable future through continuous curation. It defines what will come, what will disappear, what will return and what will be treated as an event. It projects images of performance, reward and future experience without giving the consumer, in the same measure, real conditions of verification and control.
Why does it matter to the regime?

It is not a marketing ornament. It is a technique for governing time, which monetizes expectation as a regular form of maintaining value and changes the logic by which the consumer decides and stays. This conversion of expectation into present value is what makes it economically relevant for immaterial objects of consumption.

Hypercuratorial anticipation, in this sense, is not a marketing ornament, but a technique for governing time that monetizes expectation as a regular form of maintaining value. <1>Can you check what changed?</1><2>Open auditability</2>
An item was altered, a rule changed, an account was penalized. Most of the time, the user has no way of knowing what happened, when, why and with what effect. The platform knows.

It controls the design of the environment, the criteria for changes, the system records, the moment each thing changes and even the means by which you will notice the change. That is why it has more than the power to change things. It also has the power to tell the story of what happened on its own. You are left with its version, and any challenge becomes your word against theirs.
Open auditability is thus born as a direct response to the functional opacity typical of IOCs.<1>p. 636</1>

If the supplier controls the architecture, the criteria for change, the relevant logs, the timing of the change and the very means by which the modification will be perceived, it concentrates not only the power of reconfiguration, but also the power to give a unilateral account of what occurred.<1>p. 636</1>
with structural asymmetries of challenge and proof<1>p. 393</1>
<1>Open auditability</1>

To audit is to check, and the concept describes a standard of transparency that actually serves a purpose. It is the requirement of minimum conditions so that judges, experts, consumer protection bodies and, to a certain extent, consumers themselves can reconstruct the story of what happened. This story connects what was promised, what changed, the penalty applied, the effect on use and the justification the company gave. It is worth understanding where it comes from. It is not a new law with its own name, nor a right that came out of nowhere. It is an offshoot of duties that consumer law already imposes, such as the duty to inform, good faith and making it easier for consumers to defend their rights. Its purpose is to keep information from fulfilling its role only on paper, hidden in enormous documents, notices and update histories that no one can find or connect to what happened.

Open auditability means the existence of minimum conditions of verifiability regarding relevant aspects of supply, so that protection bodies, the Judiciary, experts and, to a certain extent, consumers themselves can reconstruct the relationship between promise, alteration, sanction, functional impact and the justification presented by the supplier.<1>p. 727</1>
A closed black box with a window cut into one corner, through which some gears can be seen. Not the whole box opened, just enough to see what changed.
What if only one driver had the cameras?

Who tells the story of a traffic accident? If only one of the drivers had access to the cameras, the marks on the asphalt and the car's records, their version would be the only one that could be proven.

On a platform this is the default. Whoever controls the design, the criteria, the records and the timing of a change also controls the account of what happened. Without minimum trails, only one side's narrative exists. Open auditability is what gives the story more than one witness again.
It puts the conflict back on reconstructible ground and prevents the lack of access to evidence from turning into a practical impossibility of protection<1>p. 642</1>
What needs to be within your reach?
What needs to be within reach is simple to say. What changed, when it changed, why it changed, what effect the change had and which records allow the case to be reconstructed.

No one is asking for the company's secrets or the game's code. What is asked for is a demonstrable minimum, enough to see whether a relevant change occurred, link it to what was promised and check whether it was justified and respected predictability, proportionality and the chance to challenge it. In a dispute, there are tools to reach this minimum, such as orders to preserve and disclose records, expert examination on defined points and, depending on the case, presumptions against the company.

What is needed is sufficient intelligibility to identify the occurrence of a relevant alteration, relate it to the promised enjoyment, verify whether there was a justification compatible with the legal regime and ascertain whether the sanction, change or modulation respected minimum standards of predictability, proportionality and contestability.<1>p. 728</1>
The institutional consequence includes orders to preserve and disclose records, delimited expert examination, presumptions unfavorable to the supplier<1>p. 745</1>
Who holds the records of a conflict?

In a dispute over an item or an account, almost everything that shows what happened is in the supplier's hands. The system logs, the screen trails, the change history, the penalty criteria and the internal support conversations all sit on the other side.

This is the normal situation in these disputes, not an exception. Whoever controls these traces largely controls what can be reconstructed later. Open auditability seeks to balance precisely this concentration.
What becomes open to challenge?

As a result, what is decided inside closed systems becomes open to challenge. Another concept depends directly on this one, functional value equivalence. If you cannot reconstruct what changed, to what extent, why and when, you cannot show that you lost the equivalence of what you bought.
[...] including with regard to access rules, delivery modulations and sanction mechanisms, so as to make contestable what is produced by opaque systems<1>p. 393</1>

Without auditability, functional equivalence becomes hard to demonstrate, because the consumer cannot reconstruct what was altered, to what extent, with what motivation and at what moment.<1>p. 638</1>
Does the game's code have to be opened?

It does not mean opening the program's code, exposing all of the company's technology or doing away with trade secrets. It is not total transparency. It is sufficient transparency, minimum verifiability.

Nor does it apply to every small adjustment, purely cosmetic change or minor fluctuation. The duty begins when the alteration, the penalty or the rule change significantly affects what you use, your continued presence or your chance to prove and challenge.
The expression does not designate unrestricted opening of source code, full exposure of the technological architecture or a generalized waiver of trade secrets.<1>p. 727</1>
Not total transparency, but sufficient transparency. Not absolute disclosure, but minimum verifiability.<1>p. 728</1>

Functional value equivalence · Concepts · Lex Plataformae
<1>And when an update takes away what you bought?</1><2>Functional value equivalence</2>
Digital services change all the time, and that is normal. A game needs a new graphics engine, balance tweaks and compatibility with different computers.

But sometimes, after an update, the item is still there yet no longer does what it used to do. It has lost a function, lost the place it held among other players or lost the meaning it had for the person who bought it. You still have the account, you still see the item and you still log into the game, and yet you have lost what mattered most.

For this reason, functional value equivalence is a criterion of stability of the performance program, not a requirement that the object stand still. It makes it possible to recognize the sophisticated obvious: continuous digital services change, but they cannot change in just any way<1>p. 655</1>
The consumer does not lose merely "a feature"; they lose the functional substance of what they bought<1>p. 672</1>
<1>Functional value equivalence</1>

It is the test that asks whether, after the change, the product still plays the same role in your experience. The test is demanding. It is not enough for the item to keep working, or to keep the same numbers in some isolated attribute. What counts is the whole role it used to play. That includes its concrete usefulness in the game, the place it holds among other users and, when this matters to the law, what it means to the person who has it. An item may stay in the account and open normally and still have lost whatever justified the purchase.
A two-pan scale with the same piece of armor in each pan, the one from before and the one from after, identical on the outside. The pan holding the after version rises, because it weighs less.
Paying for a full semester and getting half a course?

A course that cuts half its classes in the middle of the semester and keeps charging the same price is doing what anyone would call wrong. Consumer law treats as void any clause that lets the supplier change, on its own, the content or quality of what it sells.

On platforms, the cut rarely goes by that name. It shows up as smaller reach, performance downgraded little by little, features that gradually disappear, tighter limits or use that costs more to deliver the same thing. The label and the price stay the same while what you get shrinks. The logic is the same as with the course.
How do you compare the before and the after?

To run the test, you compare the before and the after. You examine the versions that matter and identify the core of the usefulness that was hit. Then you assess the object's role in the experience, looking at its usefulness, the place it holds among the others and, when it matters, what it means.

A few questions help. Did the update remove an important function? Did it weaken the item to the point that it lost the usefulness you paid for? Did it change the screen in a way that disrupts everyday use? Did it rewrite rules in a way that downgrades what had been promised as equivalent? If the answer is yes, the platform was free to change, but it should have preserved the value of what you had or made room for restoration. And you do not need to prove you fully own the item in order to complain about it.
When does a phone update stop being an improvement?

A phone update may, in the name of improvement, leave the device slow or incompatible with apps while it is still within the lifespan you could expect of it. No serious person claims that every update is illegal.

The question lies elsewhere. It is whether the update significantly impaired use without adequate information, without genuine consent and without a way out for the people harmed. With a digital item, the structure is the same.

The example of updates that degrade accessibility and compatibility in software or firmware helps to visualize the structure of the problem. In these cases, no one seriously argues that every update is unlawful.<1>p. 655</1>

What is at issue is whether, under the pretext of improvement, the update significantly compromises the use, performance or compatibility of goods still within their expected durability, without adequate information, without effective consent and without mitigating avenues<1>p. 655</1>
The legal structure is the same in IOCs<1>p. 655</1>
The item still exists, but is it the one you bought?
An object may go on existing and still no longer be what was bought. That is the loss the test brings to light.

It also changes the conversation when the company says it was just an update, an adjustment or an evolution of the service. From that point on, what matters is showing that the essence of what you bought was preserved, not how technically complex the change was. When equivalence is lost, the first response is to give the function back, by undoing the change where possible, offering something equivalent or fixing the way updates are made, and not just to pay money.
So is changing things illegal?
Changing is not illegal. The test does not freeze the service or require the new version to be identical to the old one. Digital environments need to evolve, adapt and, quite often, rebalance.

What it rejects is change used to shift onto you the cost of seriously worsening what you bought, without restoration to match. And if the change is only cosmetic and the symbolic value was not at the core of what was sold, it is, as a rule, left out.

This does not mean requiring perfect identity between earlier and later versions, nor imposing a freeze on the service. Continuous digital environments presuppose evolution, adaptation and, in many cases, internal rebalancing.<1>p. 730</1>
And when equivalence is lost, what should happen? Your money back, or what you bought back?
What does functional value equivalence control?

It controls whether unilateral alterations to continuous digital services are lawful. It is the material core of the control over mutability, and it also guides the remedy. What must be preserved is the role the object played in the experience acquired, taking into account its concrete usefulness in the environment, its relational place in use and, when legally relevant, its identity or symbolic weight.
It also serves to guide remedies.<1>p. 731</1>

Functional value equivalence operates as a criterion of lawfulness of the unilateral alterations carried out in continuous digital services that administer Immaterial Objects of Consumption.<1>p. 648</1>
Functional value equivalence, therefore, constitutes the material core of the control of mutability in immaterial objects of consumption.<1>p. 731</1>
What does it not prohibit?

Change is not unlawful in itself. The criterion requires neither perfect identity between the earlier and later versions nor a freeze on the service. Mutability is legitimate when it substantially preserves the function the object serves in the consumer's experience.
